column5: Too many forces at play - effects likely to be heterogeneous for different high-skilled occupations.
column8: Again, this is too general a statement. Investment in general skills (with a strong technological component) is likely to continue to have high returns. But some specific educational programs (e.g., translation services) will see their returns diminish.

column5: Not sure whether the high-skilled or medium-skilled will be more affected.
this indeed seems likely, in contrast to earlier GPTs
column8: yes, people will have to think harder about where the jobs will be.
column11: to the extent that they eliminate some college level jobs, and potentially allow workers with less education to do more complex jobs, it seems to go the other way.

column5: While this is possible, it is also uncertain. AI can lead to a decline in the college premium as a lot of routine cognitive tasks are automatized (which may be desirable compared to earnings for the low-education workers) but AI is likely to also generate more superstars
column11: Inequality between workers (superstars vs rest), but also inequality between labor vs capital income, and profits

column5: There clearly is something new about AI relative to previous "skill biased technological change" - the skills that will be made redundant are non-routine, cognitive skills, as opposed to routine skills.
column8: It is really hard to guide your human capital investments in a world where machines are increasingly "creative" and "skilled". Areas such as computer programming, accounting or advertising will be affected, but not clear what will be the new emergent tasks.
column11: It seems AI is more likely to help less skilled workers get to the level of more skilled ones- everyone can write a decent law memo. IT also seems likely some highly skilled professions will be highly impacted.

column5: In the past, technological advances often acted as complement for high-skilled workers, increasing their value in market place. Key question is if AI is substantially different from prior technological advance. Unclear in my mind. See also survey below.
column8: In near term, this is likely correct, but not clear in long-run. Education and required knowledge will adapt and uncertainty over returns to education likely subside.
column11: Using the evidence for automation as a gauge (see below), I agree, though the effect might take longer than 10 years to be substantial.

column5: Negative for some, positive for others.
I believe the impact will be highly heterogeneous and it depends on where you set the cut off for "high skilled".
column8: AI will probably increase the mean return to education but there will be more heterogeneity across fields and across people within a field.
High-skilled individuals replaced by AI will find other jobs
column11: AI cuts both ways for inequality. College premium might fall on average but inequality will increase among high-skilled individuals

column5: Even the tasks of higher educated people (estate agents, lawyers, programmers, etc.) can be lightened or taken over by AI.
